fact_claims.verbatim: Northwind recorded 8.6 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide.
Our highest-incident model was Hearth 10, at 6.4 per 100,000 installed units.
Hearth 10’s 55 °C sustained-heat test failure rate was 6.2%.

S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, property damage, or emergency-service response to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a complete incident report within 10 business days. The manufacturer must notify affected customers within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible product-specific hazard or requires an immediate safety action.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Before purchase, customers must receive that model's test results, including the failure rate and sample size, in clear language. These customer disclosures must be made directly to prospective customers; they do not require public publication of an individual company's per-model failure rates. A failure rate above 5% requires prompt regulator notification, a corrective-action plan, and retesting; it does not by itself prohibit sale.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: Newly installed home battery systems must support secure remote emergency shut-off by 1 January 2028, with a safe local shut-off option available to occupants and emergency responders. Existing installed units must be upgraded or replaced to support remote shut-off within six years of this standard taking effect, where technically feasible; manufacturers must provide customers with a documented upgrade plan and disclose any units that cannot be upgraded.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New home battery units manufactured 36 months or more after this standard takes effect must include built-in fire suppression meeting regulator-approved performance and reliability requirements.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: A manufacturer must initiate a regulator-supervised recall when a model's verified thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 per 100,000 installed units in any year. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of credible product-specific hazards and provide updated instructions and corrective actions; urgent hazards require notice within 48 hours of determination.

document.section_notes: S1 is strong: all incidents (including minor overheating/smoke) reportable to the regulator within 24h, customer hazard notice within 48h, no phase-in. S2 sets a 55 °C test and a 5% failure rate but explicitly says exceeding it 'does not by itself prohibit sale', so the cap is only a notification/corrective-action trigger (no sales stop) - weakened, though per-model numeric results do reach purchasers without public publication, satisfying both NW-1 and HC-1. S3 keeps new-unit shut-off (fixed 1 Jan 2028 date, not expressed in months) with a 72-month retrofit window and a feasibility escape that still requires an upgrade plan and disclosure; S4 mandates built-in suppression at 36 months (HC-2 satisfied); S5 keeps a mandatory numeric 8/100k recall trigger with no phase-in and 48h notice, but omits any serious-injury recall clause.
